title: Settings in a CRM
excerpt: Settings are a cabinet, not a second product. Group what a salesperson changes often between calls, and bury the rest where it belongs.
alt: A glass-walled office corridor with a sofa, a floor lamp, and black pendant lights, a hallway you pass through rather than a room you live in.
caption: An office corridor with a sofa and a lamp, a place you pass through. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in CRM settings?
faqs.answer: Settings are a cabinet for things the salesperson changes rarely, plus a few personal preferences they change more often. Notifications, the fields on their own card, and a signature belong near the front. Pipeline admin, integrations, and permissions for the whole company belong in a deeper drawer most reps should not have to walk past.

faqs.question: Should settings open as a full product?
faqs.answer: No. A second navigation, a second home, and a tour of settings means you have built two products. Open the cabinet, show a short list grouped by how often the person changes it, and return them to the record they came from. The record is the product.

faqs.question: Who should see admin settings?
faqs.answer: Only the people who can safely change a setting should see it. A rep's cabinet is personal preferences, and an admin's cabinet adds the shared pipeline. Mixing them on one long page is how a rep changes a team-wide stage by accident.

markdown:
CRM settings UX should feel like opening a cabinet, not launching a second product. Group what the salesperson, the one updating a record between calls, changes often. Bury the rest. The record is the work. Settings are where the work goes when something about the tool itself must change, and then the person should come back.

If settings has its own dashboard, its own tour, and its own empty states about "getting started," you have lost the plot.

## A cabinet, not a home

A cabinet has drawers. You open one, you take the thing, you close it. You do not redecorate your day inside it. The CRM settings page should behave the same way. A short list, plain names, and a way back to the record that was on screen a second ago. The draft note is still there when they return. If it is not, settings is dangerous and people will refuse to open it, which means they will live with the wrong notification settings forever.

Do not give settings a hero. No illustration of a well-organized life. No progress bar of "profile completeness." Those patterns come from consumer apps that need to harvest data. A salesperson's profile is complete enough when the note saves and the right people get the follow-up. Completeness widgets create fake work between calls. Ban them from this cabinet.

Name the drawers in their language. "Notifications." "My card." "Email." "The pipeline," if they are allowed to see it. Not "Workspace configuration" and "Entity preferences." If a label needs a glossary, it is the wrong label for a cabinet. Cabinets are labeled for the person in a hurry, which is the only person you have.

[The WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) puts understandable next to perceivable, operable, and robust, and it applies to web applications. Settings are where products become hard to understand: long forms, controls that change other screens, and labels written by the team that built the data model. Group related controls. Give every control a label that says what it changes, not a key from the API. Make sure the focus order follows the drawers. A cabinet that can only be used with a precise mouse path is not a cabinet. It is a puzzle.

## What they change often

Put the frequent things in the first drawer, and make that drawer short.

Notifications are the real setting. Which events interrupt a call, which can wait for the end of the day, which should never be a push. A rep who is notified of every stage change in the company will mute the product, and then they will miss the one mention that mattered. Default to quiet. Let them add the few events that are actually theirs: a note on their deal, a meeting in the next hour, a reply.

The fields on their own working card come next. Some reps need the phone number large. Some need the last note. Let them choose a small set, from a list you bless, rather than offering every column in the database. A free arrangement of forty fields is how the first screen you carefully stripped gets reassembled as clutter. Constraints are a kindness. "Choose up to four facts under the name" is a setting. A blank canvas is an abandonment.

Signature and send-from address belong here if email leaves from the CRM. They change rarely, but when they are wrong they are wrong on every message. One screen, a preview of the message, and a save that says it applies to the next email, not to the one already sent. Do not bury the signature under "integrations" because email happens to use an integration. Bury the integration. Surface the signature.

Time zone and working hours are frequent in a team that sells across regions, and invisible until a meeting lands at 5 a.m. Put them in this first drawer. Show an example: "Meetings will display in Central Time." An example prevents the class of bug where the control was saved and the calendar still looks wrong because they did not understand the label.

## What to bury

Bury team-wide pipeline stages, required fields for the whole company, roles, API keys, and anything that changes another person's first screen. These are admin acts. They can live in the same product, behind a clear door, not interleaved with "my signature."

A rep who can see the admin drawers but not use them should not scroll past a graveyard of locks to find their notifications. Give them a cabinet without those drawers. Give the admin a cabinet that contains the personal drawers and, separately, the shared ones. The shared ones should say, at the top, that changes affect everyone. A sentence like "This changes the stages every rep sees" prevents more accidents than a confirmation dialog people have learned to dismiss.

Integrations are the deepest drawer. Connecting a mailbox can be legitimate. A page that lists twenty logos, most of them irrelevant, is a marketplace posing as settings. If you have one integration a rep needs, put that task in the first drawer as a task, "Connect your calendar," and leave the marketplace to admins. Do not let a logo grid become the first impression of the cabinet.

Billing for the CRM itself, seats, and invoices for your own product do not belong in the salesperson's cabinet at all. That is a finance or admin surface. Mixing "upgrade your plan" with "quiet my notifications" is how a rep opens settings and feels sold to. Sell somewhere else. This cabinet is for doing the job.

Import and export are buried, and they are labeled with their danger. Export of the whole book is not a personal preference. It is an event. Confirm it, log it, and do not put it next to the signature where a mis-tap is plausible.

## Defaults that respect the gap

The default cabinet, on the first day, should already be right enough that a rep does not have to visit it before their first note. Defaults are the real design. Settings are the escape hatch. If everyone must open settings before the product works, you shipped a setup wizard and called it a cabinet.

Quiet notifications. A card with name, company, next step, and note. A time zone from the company, adjustable. No required tour of settings. You can mention, once, that notifications can be changed, in a sentence on the first screen after a noisy event, not before they have done anything.

When you add a new setting, resist putting it in the first drawer because you are proud of it. Ask how often a rep between calls would change it. If the answer is "never," it is admin or it is not a setting. If the answer is "once a year," bury it. The first drawer is a scarce shelf. A scarce shelf stays usable.

Write down the default in the same place as the control. "Default: off." Support will ask. The rep will ask. A control with no stated default becomes folklore, and folklore is how two reps end up with contradictory advice about the same checkbox.

## Dangerous settings

Some settings change history, not just the future. Renaming a stage, merging two fields, or making a field required. These need a preview of the damage. "14 open deals use the stage you are renaming." A rename box alone is how you rewrite the past by accident. Show the count. Delay the apply. Let an admin do it, not a rep who wandered into the wrong drawer.

Destructive settings get the same treatment as destructive actions on a record. Name the object. Avoid "Are you sure?" Prefer "Rename 'Negotiation' to 'Proposal' on 14 deals." If you cannot state the effect, you do not understand it well enough to ship the control.

Personal settings that feel safe can still be sharp. Changing the email sender affects the next hundred notes. Show the preview. Changing notification sound to something continuous is a prank they will play on themselves. Prefer a small set of choices to a file upload of an arbitrary sound. Cabinets should not contain toys.

Audit the dangerous ones. An admin should be able to see who changed the pipeline and when. That log is not the rep's first drawer. It is part of the admin drawer, and it is how you undo a mistake without a backup drill. If there is no undo, say so before they apply. "This cannot be undone" is allowed only when it is true, and it should sit next to a count, not alone as atmosphere.

## Returning to the record

Every path out of settings should land on the record they left, not on a settings home, and not on the CRM's marketing dashboard. The back control, the save confirmation, and the logo should agree. A logo that goes to the dashboard from inside settings is a trap. They will lose the thread of the call they were logging.

Save explicitly when the change is shared or dangerous. Autosave the harmless personal ones, and say that you did. "Notifications saved" as a small confirmation is enough. A full-page success state is the second product again. Do not celebrate a checkbox.

If a setting cannot be changed from the phone, say so, and do not offer a broken form. Many between-call sessions are on a phone. The first drawer should work there. The admin drawers can be honest about needing a desk. Honesty is a label: "Pipeline changes are available on a larger screen." A shrunk desktop form that requires horizontal scrolling is not a mobile cabinet. It is a refusal to choose.

## How you know the cabinet is too big

Count the items in the first drawer. If there are more than a handful, you have not buried enough. Watch a new rep try to turn down noise. Time it. If they pass through integrations, billing, and roles on the way to notifications, the information architecture is a hallway you built to store your roadmap.

Listen for the sentence "where do I change…?" in support. Each question is a label you missed or a drawer you buried too well. The frequent questions belong in the first drawer with the words the question used. The rare questions can stay deep. Do not promote a setting to the front because one person could not find it once, if the cost is clutter for everyone else. Improve the label where it sits, first.

A cabinet that stays small is a product decision. Say no to a screen for every team that asks for a place in settings. Many of those requests are really a field on the record. Put it there if it belongs to the gap between calls.

The same cabinet problem shows up in tools where the fear is a wrong charge rather than a lost note. [The first screen of a billing tool](/blog/the-first-screen-of-a-billing-tool) is the next piece, because a finance lead who is afraid of a wrong invoice also needs one object and one action, and a tour is just as wrong there.
